summary: This informational document describes a backward-compatible technique for OSPF implementations to advertise that a router cannot forward transit traffic, or to make paths through it less preferred. It obsoletes RFC 3137.

eli5.summary: A router can raise a sign saying "do not drive through me, I am busy," while still being reachable itself.

questions: how to take an ospf router out of transit path
what is an ospf stub router
how to stop transit traffic through an ospf router
subtitle: How an OSPF router can say 'do not route through me' while still being reachable itself.

tldr.problem: Sometimes a router should stay in the network but not carry other routers' traffic, for example when it is overloaded or being brought in or out of service.
tldr.mechanism: The router sends its router-LSA with the cost of every non-stub link set to MaxLinkMetric (0xffff), so other routers route around it but can still reach its own prefixes. OSPFv3 can instead clear the R-bit.
tldr.outcome: This is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 3137 and is itself updated by later RFCs. It adds the MaxLinkMetric constant and the R-bit option.

today: RFC 6987 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 3137. It is updated by RFC 8770 and RFC 10041.

sections.title: Why Hide a Router from Transit Traffic
sections.content:
Sometimes it helps to tell the routers in a network not to use one router as a transit point while still being able to route to it. The RFC lists three situations: the router is in a critical condition (very high CPU load, or not enough memory to store all Link State Advertisements or build the routing table), graceful introduction and removal of the router, and other administrative or traffic engineering reasons.

The technique does not remove the router from the topology view, which flushing its router-LSA would do. Other routers are discouraged from using it for transit, while packets for the router's own IP addresses still reach it, so the router is announced as a stub. The RFC stresses that the benefit is real in networks with some redundancy, so traffic can be routed around the stub router. Otherwise, traffic for networks reachable only through it may still go through it.
sections.eli5: A busy shop can ask people not to walk through it as a shortcut, while still welcoming customers. That only helps if there is another way around.

sections.title: How the Stub Router Announces Itself
sections.content:
Call the router that wants to become a stub router X. The solution has to do two things: make other routers prefer routes around X during the Dijkstra calculation, and still let them reach IP prefixes directly connected to X.

Simply flushing X's router-LSA would cover the first goal but not the second. Other routers could not use links to X in Dijkstra (there would be no back link), and X would have no links to its neighbors. So X instead announces its router-LSA with the cost of all non-stub links (links of types other than 3) set to MaxLinkMetric. This applies to both OSPFv2 (RFC 2328) and OSPFv3 (RFC 5340).
sections.eli5: The router does not vanish from the map. It just marks all its roads as 'very expensive', so travelers pick other roads, but its own front door stays reachable.

sections.title: The MaxLinkMetric Value
sections.content:
MaxLinkMetric is a new fixed architectural value introduced by this document. It is the metric value that says a router-LSA link should not be used for transit traffic, and it is defined as the 16-bit binary value of all ones: 0xffff.

Appendix A explains the purpose: a named constant removes confusion about how to interpret LSInfinity.
sections.eli5: It is a special 'biggest possible price' label that every router recognizes as 'please do not use'.

sections.title: The OSPFv3 R-bit Alternative
sections.content:
OSPFv3 has additional options for similar control of the forwarding topology. The R-bit indicates whether a router is active and should be used for transit traffic. A router that clears it stops being used for transit.

The RFC leaves it to network operators to decide which technique to use in their network.
sections.eli5: OSPFv3 also has an on/off switch that says 'this router is not for passing through', which is a clearer way to say the same thing.

sections.title: Deployment and Security Notes
sections.content:
Routers differ in how they treat a MaxLinkMetric link. Routers that follow the intra-area Dijkstra calculation of RFC 1247 discard link records with that cost. Routers that follow RFC 1583 and higher do not treat such links as unreachable. This inconsistency does not cause routing loops: if alternate paths exist, both kinds of router agree to use them. If the path through the stub router is the only one, the first kind will not use it for transit, which is the desired behavior, but the second kind still will.

Clearing the R-bit consistently results in the router not being used for transit. So the choice depends on the operator's goal: MaxLinkMetric allows the only available path to be used, while the R-bit does not.

The Security Considerations section says the technique does not introduce any new security issues into OSPF.
sections.eli5: Some older routers ignore the 'expensive' label and use the road anyway when there is no other way. The on/off switch is stricter. Pick the one that fits what you want.
